clips.title: Stateful vs Stateless Architectures Explained
clips.why: The idea behind this lesson in two and a half minutes: a stateful server remembers things between requests, a stateless one keeps them somewhere shared.
look: What goes wrong in the stateful version when the server that remembered you is gone.
Where the stateless version keeps the session instead.
The online shopping example: swap "cart" for "which run owns this thread".
clips.after: Our Slack app is the stateless kind: the thread record lives with the broker and the status lives in the run, so any copy of the app can handle any reply.

clips.title: Build an AI Slack Bot Tutorial
clips.why: A short tour of the Slack side: configuring an app, its permissions and event subscriptions, then a small backend that reacts to messages.
look: Which events the app subscribes to, because a message in a thread only reaches an app that asked for message events.
How Slack reaches the backend in the video. Ours uses Socket Mode instead: the app opens the connection to Slack, so we publish no URL.
The handler receiving an event and replying in Slack.
clips.after: Our app subscribes to messages in the Nova channel the same way, but its handler sends a Temporal signal instead of calling a model.

clips.title: Stateful vs Stateless Architecture Explained with Real-World Examples
clips.why: Why stateless is the safer choice for something that is restarted and scaled often: any copy can serve any request, and losing one copy loses nothing.
look: Reliability: a failed server takes no data with it.
The failure points a stateful design adds.
clips.after: A deploy of the Slack app in the middle of a question is a normal Tuesday, so the app must be the kind of service where losing a copy loses nothing.

practice.q: Which of these Slack events should the handler turn into answerQuestion?

options.text: Nova's own question in the thread, which Slack also sends to the app
options.why: It has a bot_id. Without that check, Nova would answer itself.

options.text: Your edit of an earlier reply (subtype message_changed)
options.why: Messages with a subtype are edits, joins and other system events, not new answers.
A person, no subtype, and a thread_ts that the broker knows: exactly what an answer looks like.

options.text: Your new message in the channel, outside any thread
options.why: No thread_ts, so it belongs to no run.

practice.q: Finish the first line of the reply handler.
practice.hint: The field Slack sets on messages written by apps.
practice.why: bot_id marks a message from a bot, Nova's own messages included, so only people's replies become answers.

practice.q: Put the path of your reply in order.
items: Slack sends the app a message event with the thread's thread_ts
The app acknowledges and checks: a person, no subtype, inside a thread
The app asks the broker which run owns the thread
The app signals answerQuestion to nova:RH-1234 with the text and your email
Temporal stores the signal in the run's history, and the handler adds the reply to the list
The VM wakes and the session resumes with all replies joined
practice.why: The address comes from the event and one lookup, and once Temporal has stored the signal the reply is safe.

practice.q: Where does /nova status RH-1234 get its answer?

options.text: From a query to the run nova:RH-1234
options.why: The worker answers from the run's current state, so the answer is always current and the app stores nothing.

options.text: From the last status the app posted, kept in a variable
options.why: That copy is gone after a restart and may be stale. The run is the source of the truth.

options.text: From the text of the status message in Slack
options.why: The message shows the state, but reading it back from Slack makes Slack the source of truth, which it is not.

practice.q: Finish the signal handler so that a second reply does not erase the first.
practice.hint: Add to the end of the list instead of replacing it.
practice.why: People answer in pieces. Each reply is added to the list, and the run joins them all when the session resumes; storing only the latest one would lose the earlier answers.

practice.q: You click Approve, and Temporal cannot be reached. What should the app do?

options.text: Keep the decision in memory and send it when Temporal is back
options.why: A restart in between would lose it, and nobody would know.

options.text: Tell you, in a message only you can see, that it did not reach Nova and to try again
options.why: A decision must never disappear silently. The person can try again, and the buttons stay until a decision really arrives.

options.text: Remove the buttons so he cannot click twice
options.why: Then the decision is lost and the plan can never be approved from Slack.
